title: Roofing Over an Alleyway, Then: Does a Sukkah Need to Feel Permanent?
subtitle: Two more borrowed-wall cases, the sun/shade rule refined, and a wide list of Tannaim united by one requirement — dirat keva.
sources: Gemara text: Sefaria (William Davidson Edition). Structure and quiz questions 3, 5-6 cross-checked against the Dafyomi Advancement Forum (dafyomi.co.il) quiz for Sukkah 7. Tosfos: dafyomi.co.il's "Point by Point Summary of Tosfos" (Yaakov Montrose, Kollel Iyun Hadaf). The round-sukkah geometry question continues onto 8a.
before: 7a closed by asking whether sukkah-law ever lends a leniency back to Shabbos-law without needing to say so explicitly. This amud opens with two concrete examples — roofing over an alleyway's side-post, and roofing over the symbolic posts around a well — both borrowed from Shabbos-partition law to validate a sukkah.

From there the amud pivots to the sun/shade rule (does it matter whether excess sunlight comes through the roofing or through gaps in the walls?), and then to a much bigger unifying idea: a long list of Tannaim who all seem to require a sukkah to feel like a genuinely permanent dwelling — even though the Mishnah's own plain reading calls it dirat arai, a temporary one.

Does that include sunlight leaking through the walls, or only through the sechach?

items.sub: wall-gaps count too — derived from the Torah calling the Ark's curtain "sechach"

flowCaption: Two more validated shortcuts, a refined sun/shade rule, then the big-picture question of what a sukkah is supposed to feel like.

opinions.claim: Excess sunlight invalidates a sukkah whether it comes through the sechach or through gaps in the walls — a wall has to function like sechach in that respect too.
opinions.basis: The Torah calls the Ark's curtain (a partition, not a roof) "sechach" (Exodus 40:3) — so a partition must share the roofing's light-blocking standard.

opinions.claim: Only sunlight coming through the roofing counts toward the sun/shade calculation — wall-gaps are irrelevant.
opinions.basis: Read "vesakkota" (you shall screen) as merely requiring the curtain to be bent slightly so it visually resembles roofing — not as importing roofing's full legal standard.

opinions.claim: A wide range of positions — Rabbi, Rabbi Yoshiya, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Shimon, Rabban Gamliel, Beit Shammai, Rabbi Eliezer, and Acherim — all share one underlying intuition: a sukkah should be built and treated like a genuinely permanent dwelling, even though the base-line halachah calls it temporary.
opinions.basis: Each position is read as applying that same intuition at a different threshold or in a different area (minimum size, maximum height, wall count, mobility, roof, corners).

script.speaker: First case
script.quote: סִיכֵּךְ עַל גַּבֵּי מָבוֹי שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ לֶחִי — כְּשֵׁרָה.
script.gloss: Roofing placed over an alleyway that already has a side-post (lechi) for Shabbos purposes is a valid sukkah.

script.speaker: Second case
script.quote: סִיכֵּךְ עַל גַּבֵּי פַּסֵּי בֵירָאוֹת — כְּשֵׁרָה.
script.gloss: Roofing placed over the symbolic corner-posts surrounding a public well (a leniency for festival pilgrims) is also a valid sukkah — even though those posts are far from real walls.

script.speaker: Why both are needed
script.gloss: The alleyway case alone might be explained by its two genuine full walls. The well-post case alone might be explained by its symbolic "four walls." Neither case proves the general principle without the other.

script.speaker: New mishnah clause
script.gloss: Also invalid: a sukkah with more sunlight than shade.

script.speaker: Beraita specifies
script.quote: חֲמָתָהּ מֵחֲמַת סִיכּוּךְ, וְלֹא מֵחֲמַת דְּפָנוֹת. רַבִּי יֹאשִׁיָּה אוֹמֵר: אַף מֵחֲמַת דְּפָנוֹת.
script.gloss: The sun/shade rule is about sunlight from the roofing, not from the walls. Rabbi Yoshiya disagrees: it includes wall-driven sunlight too.

script.speaker: Answered
script.quote: וְסַכּוֹתָ עַל הָאָרוֹן אֶת הַפָּרוֹכֶת... אַלְמָא מְחִיצָה כִּסְכָךְ בָּעֵינַן.
script.gloss: "And you shall screen (vesakkota) the Ark with the curtain" — a curtain is a partition, yet the Torah calls covering it with a curtain "sekhakha" (roofing language). This shows a partition must meet the same light-blocking standard as roofing.

script.speaker: The Rabbis' reading
script.quote: הַהוּא דְּנִיכּוֹף בַּיהּ פּוּרְתָּא, דְּמִחֲזֵי כִּסְכָךְ.
script.gloss: That verse just means bend the curtain slightly so it visually resembles roofing — not that walls inherit the roofing's full halachic standard.

script.speaker: Abaye's wide survey
script.quote: רַבִּי, וְרַבִּי יֹאשִׁיָּה, וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן, וְרַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל, וּבֵית שַׁמַּאי, וְרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר, וַאֲחֵרִים — כּוּלְּהוּ סְבִירָא לְהוּ: סוּכָּה דִּירַת קֶבַע בָּעֵינַן.
script.gloss: Abaye: a whole list of Tannaim converge on requiring a sukkah to resemble a permanent dwelling — Rabbi (4×4 amos minimum), Rabbi Yoshiya (walls block sun like sechach), Rabbi Yehuda (validates >20 amos, since permanence is fine), Rabbi Shimon (four walls), Rabban Gamliel (invalidates a wagon/boat sukkah), Beit Shammai (rejects a too-small sukkah), Rabbi Eliezer (requires an actual roof), and Acherim (requires corners, rejecting a round dovecote-shaped sukkah).

script.speaker: Rabbi Yochanan, on round sukkahs
script.quote: סוּכָּה הָעֲשׂוּיָה כְּכִבְשָׁן, אִם יֵשׁ בְּהֶקֵּיפָהּ כְּדֵי לֵישֵׁב בָּהּ עֶשְׂרִים וְאַרְבָּעָה בְּנֵי אָדָם — כְּשֵׁרָה.
script.gloss: A furnace-shaped (fully round) sukkah is valid only if its circumference fits 24 people — matching Rabbi's 4×4-amos-square standard, converted to a circle.

script.speaker: Gemara does the math, continuing to 8a
script.quote: מִכְּדִי, גַּבְרָא בְּאַמְּתָא יָתֵיב... בִּתְרֵיסַר סַגִּי?
script.gloss: Wait — if each person takes up roughly a cubit, and every 3 tefachim of circumference corresponds to about 1 tefach of diameter, the math should only require a 12-person circumference to match a 4-amos square, not 24. Why does Rabbi Yochanan require double? Continued on 8a.

tosfos.dh: תוספות ד״ה סיכך על גבי מבוי
tosfos.summary: Rashi and Tosfos disagree on what kind of alleyway this case is even describing, given that an alleyway only needs rabbinic-level walls while sukkah needs Torah-level ones.

points.label: (a) Question
points.he: קשה מה ענין סוכה דבעי מחיצות דאורייתא למבוי דרבנן
points.en: How can a rabbinic-level alleyway wall ever validate a Torah-level sukkah wall?

points.label: (b)-(g) Resolved through several attempts
points.he: וי"ל דמיירי בלחי טפח... ובקונטרס פי' דמיירי במבוי מפולש... וי"ל דלעולם מיירי במבוי סתום מג' רוחות
points.en: Tosfos works through several readings before landing on one: the alleyway is closed on three sides, but only roofed near the post — leaving that section of the sukkah with just two real walls plus the tefach-post, the same structure already validated earlier.

tosfos.dh: תוספות ד״ה סיכך ע״ג פסי ביראות
tosfos.summary: Why the well-post leniency (originally just for festival pilgrims' animals) can validate a sukkah for anyone.

points.label: (c) Answer
points.he: מ"מ כיון דמדאורייתא שרי בכל ענין אמרינן מגו ואפילו מדרבנן לא אסרי משום מצות סוכה
points.en: Since Torah law permits it unconditionally (the pilgrim-specific restriction is only rabbinic), the miggo argument goes through in full — and the Sages didn't restrict it further given the sukkah mitzvah.

tosfos.summary: Rebbi Yoshiya's "walls must block sun like sechach" isn't actually connected to the earlier derivation of wall-count from "ba'sukkot."

points.label: (b)-(c) Answer and proof
points.he: דהתם לא דרשינן אלא מייתורא... ותדע דכולהו מודו דלא בעינן למחיצות פסולת גורן ויקב
points.en: That earlier derivation only worked from the extra repetitions of the word — not from any claim that "sukkot" itself means walls. Proof: everyone agrees sukkah walls don't need to meet sechach's own material requirements (only actual roofing does).

tosfos.summary: If Acherim (identified as Rabbi Meir) really holds dirat keva, he likely also holds a sukkah needs a mezuzah during the festival.

points.label: (a)-(b) Connecting the dots
points.he: דסוכה דירת קבע בעינן ואחרים היינו ר"מ... כדמוכח פ"ק דיומא דמהאי טעמא מחייב רבי יהודה סוכת החג בחג במזוזה
points.en: If a sukkah must feel permanent, that same logic (used explicitly by Rabbi Yehuda in Yoma 10a) would obligate a mezuzah on the sukkah during the festival itself — consistent with treating it as a real dwelling.
